meta.audience: The believers gathered at the waters of Mormon
meta.location: The place of Mormon, in the borders of the land of Lehi-Nephi

world_behind.title: A church founded illegally
world_behind.text: Every stage of this happens out of sight. Alma teaches privately so the king will not hear of it, hides in a thicket by day, meets people at a spring in the borders of the land, and the record twice says the location was chosen so the news would not reach the court. The first congregation in this book is an underground one.

world_behind.title: The worst ground available
world_behind.text: Mormon was named by the king and named for what lived there: a place infested at seasons by wild beasts. That is exactly why it is unwatched. The believers gather at a watering hole nobody wants, and the record's own compiler centuries later carries the name of the place.

world_behind.title: The support arrangement is reversed
world_behind.text: Noah had put down his father's priests, consecrated proud ones in their place, and supported them out of a fifth-part tax. Alma ordains one priest to every fifty, forbids them to depend on the people, and makes them work for their own living. The people are asked to give, but not to the priesthood. They give to whoever is in need.

world_behind.title: Terms first, then consent
world_behind.text: Verses 8 through 10 read the covenant out in full and end with a question: what have you against being baptized? Nothing is administered before the group has heard what it costs and answered. In a colony ruled by decree, a public offer with an option to decline is itself a political statement.

world_behind.title: Where the authority came from is not explained
world_behind.text: Alma says he baptizes "having authority from the Almighty God," and the record never says when or how he received it. He had been one of Noah's own priests, consecrated by a king this record condemns. The silence is complete and the record does not seem troubled by it.

world_behind.title: A minority inside a minority
world_behind.text: Zeniff's colony already pays for its existence and sits inside Lamanite country. Alma's group is a dissenting fraction of that, and when it moves in verse 34 it takes tents and families into land no state controls.

words.text: Not secretly in the sense of concealed doctrine, but out of the authorities' view. The verse gives the reason plainly: that it might not come to the knowledge of the king. Everything taught here was already public preaching four chapters ago; only the audience has gone underground.

Overrun, occupied by something unwanted. The word is doing double duty in the verse, since the place is named for the beasts and the beasts are the reason nobody is watching it. What makes the ground worthless to the kingdom is what makes it usable.

Wanting a thing, with the wanting stated as the qualification. Alma does not ask what the group believes or what it has done. He asks whether coming into the fold of God is the desire of their hearts, and the whole covenant hangs off that clause.

In greater measure, more freely. The word governs what is promised in return: that God may pour out his Spirit more abundantly. It appears again at verse 27, where whoever has more abundantly is to give more abundantly, which puts the receiving and the giving in one vocabulary.

Appointed and set apart to an office. The ratio is given immediately, one priest to every fifty. The ordination is an administrative act with a number attached. Four priests would have covered the whole congregation at its founding size.

To give a share of something you have. It governs both directions in this chapter: the priests impart the word, the people impart their substance, and the verse sets the rate by capacity. Of him that had but little, but little should be required.

Informed, given notice. The word appears where a warning would be expected and the record uses the flat administrative term instead. Whoever told them, and however, the chapter reports only that they knew in time.

phrases.term: Bear one another's burdens, that they may be light
phrases.text: Paul writes almost the first half of this to the Galatians. What is added here is the purpose clause: sharing makes the burdens light. The covenant's first term is therefore about weight.

Paul's version of the same instruction pairs weeping with weeping and rejoicing with rejoicing. This one keeps only the grief and adds a second clause about comfort for those who need it. The covenant asks for presence in the harder direction and does not mention the easier one.

phrases.term: Stand as witnesses of God at all times and in all things, and in all places
phrases.text: Three universals stacked, and the sentence ends "even until death." The men listening had watched a witness burn not long before, and the clause is not a figure of speech to them. It occurs once in scripture.

phrases.term: What have you against being baptized in the name of the Lord
phrases.text: A question rather than a command, and phrased as an invitation to object. Alma has just finished stating the terms; this is the point at which someone could walk away. The answer comes back as applause rather than assent.

phrases.term: Only he did not bury himself again in the water
phrases.text: The record slowing down to specify what Alma did with his own body. Verse 14 has both Alma and Helam going under together; verse 15 says he did not repeat that with the next person. A small procedural detail is preserved with more care than the sermon that preceded it.

phrases.term: The church of God, or the church of Christ
phrases.text: Two names offered as alternatives, in a record that has not used the word this way before. The naming is reported as a fact rather than as an act. They were called it, from that time forward, with no account of who did the calling. Alma's son will later cite this founding by name and place.

phrases.term: Look forward with one eye, having one faith and one baptism
phrases.text: Paul's triad to Ephesus has one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Here the first item is replaced by a shared direction of gaze, and the phrase occurs once in scripture. Unity is described as facing the same way rather than as agreeing.

phrases.term: How beautiful are they to the eyes of them who there came to the knowledge of their Redeemer
phrases.text: Isaiah's line about beautiful feet on the mountains, relocated to a pool and a wood. Alma had stood in a courtroom while Abinadi expounded that verse; here the beauty has moved from the messenger to the place where the message landed. The verse says the name Mormon six times, attaching it to the place, the waters, and the forest.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: A fugitive with a manuscript
verses.text: Alma has repented, is wanted by the king's servants, and goes about privately teaching what he wrote down while hiding. The content is listed in verse 2 and it is Abinadi's outline: what was to come, the resurrection, redemption, through the sufferings and death of Christ.

verses.label: v. 4–7
verses.title: A thicket and a spring
verses.text: He hides in small trees by day and the believers come to him. The gathering is described as taking many days to assemble and as growing to a goodly number, which means people kept walking out to the borders of the land over many days without being caught.

verses.label: v. 8–10
verses.title: The terms, and then the question
verses.text: Come into the fold, be called his people, bear burdens, mourn with mourners, comfort the comfortless, witness everywhere until death. Then the reward, and then an invitation to object. The covenant is almost entirely about how these people will treat each other.

verses.label: v. 12–15
verses.title: Helam, and then everyone else
verses.text: Alma prays for himself before he touches anyone, then baptizes Helam with both of them going under. The formula he uses claims authority and states the covenant's term as "until you are dead as to the mortal body." Then the record notes what he did differently the second time.

verses.label: v. 17–22
verses.title: Named, staffed, and instructed
verses.text: They become the church; priests are ordained at one to fifty; the priests may teach only what Alma taught and what the prophets spoke; no contention; one eye, one faith, one baptism, hearts knit. The instructions are shorter than the covenant that preceded them.

verses.label: v. 24–29
verses.title: A church nobody gets paid by
verses.text: Priests work with their hands and take nothing from the congregation. Giving is redirected past the clergy to whoever is in need, described as free will and good desires, and the chapter closes the passage by saying they did walk uprightly, imparting both temporally and spiritually.

verses.label: v. 32–35
verses.title: Found out, and gone
verses.text: The king notices a movement, sends watchers, and calls the assembly a rebellion. There is no trial this time. They take their tents and families and leave, and the count has gone from two hundred and four to four hundred and fifty.

chapter.title: This is the first church in the record
chapter.text: Before verse 17 the word belongs to Nephi's vision of two churches far in the future and to one line where Zoram assumes Nephi means a congregation in Jerusalem. The first assembly of believers on this land to be called a church is an illegal one meeting at a watering hole named for wild animals.

chapter.title: It is founded on a copy
chapter.text: What Alma preaches is Abinadi's sermon, which survives only because Alma wrote it out while being hunted. Much later the Lord's own comment on this founding names the source exactly: blessed for exceeding faith in the words alone of a servant named Abinadi.

chapter.title: The covenant is stated almost entirely as obligations to other people
chapter.text: Burdens, mourning, comfort, witness. One doctrinal clause arrives at the end (redeemed of God, numbered with the first resurrection), and even that is phrased as a consequence. Nothing in the terms asks the group to affirm a proposition.

chapter.title: Every institutional rule reverses Noah's arrangement
chapter.text: Noah deposed his father's priests and consecrated proud ones supported by a fifth-part tax. Alma ordains at a fixed ratio, forbids dependence on the people, requires manual labor, forbids contention, and directs giving to the needy rather than to the clergy. The chapter never mentions Noah while doing it.

chapter.title: The most carefully preserved detail is procedural
chapter.text: The record spends a clause specifying that Alma went under the water with the first candidate and did not do so with the second. It reports the founding sermon in summary and this in full.

chapter.title: The group more than doubles inside fifteen verses
chapter.text: Two hundred and four at the baptism, four hundred and fifty at the flight. The record does not describe the growth; it only gives the two numbers and lets the difference stand.

chapter.title: The charge is political again, and this time there is no trial
chapter.text: Noah's court had to convert a doctrinal objection into "he has reviled the king" before it could execute Abinadi. Here the king skips the step and calls a religious meeting a rebellion. An army is sent instead of a summons.

chapter.title: Isaiah's beautiful feet end up on a forest floor
chapter.text: Alma had heard Abinadi expound that verse in Noah's court, where it was about a messenger arriving with news. Verse 30 gives the phrase to a pool, a wood, and the people who learned something there. It is the last thing said about the place before the king finds it.

applications.title: Write the terms down before asking for a yes
applications.text: Alma stated everything the covenant required and then invited objection. Before asking anyone to commit to something, try saying the whole cost out loud first and leaving them room to decline.

applications.title: Measure a commitment by what it obliges you to do for people
applications.text: Almost every clause is about somebody else's weight, grief, or need. When you evaluate a commitment you have made, check how much of it is about other people and how much is about your own position.

applications.title: Give by capacity
applications.text: More from those with more, little required of those with little, and something for those with nothing. It is a rule that works without anyone knowing what anyone else gave.

applications.title: Do not let the work depend on being paid for it
applications.text: The priests labored for their own support so that teaching could not become a livelihood. Where something matters to you, consider whether it would survive losing its funding.

applications.title: Take the ground nobody wants
applications.text: They met at a place named for the beasts that infested it, and it was safe precisely because it was undesirable. When you need room to start something, the overlooked option is often the only unguarded one.

applications.title: Face the same direction
applications.text: The instruction is one eye looking forward and no contention. Unity described as a shared direction is a lower bar and a more durable one.

applications.title: Notice when the objection changes shape
applications.text: The complaint against Abinadi became "he reviled the king." The complaint against Alma became "rebellion." Both started as disagreements about doctrine. Watch for the moment a disagreement gets restated as a threat.

questions.text: Whose burden have I actually made lighter this month?
Where am I willing to stand as a witness, and where do I go quiet?
What have I agreed to without ever being told the terms?
Which disagreements am I treating as contention that are only differences?
What would I keep doing if nobody supported me for it?
Which ordinary place would I call beautiful because of what I understood there?
